title: Every living thing from water
hook: We made every living thing from water (21:30)
tomorrow: Dawud and Sulayman judge a field

segments.voice: Yesterday, before sunrise and sunset, and your line was glory at both edges. Did you mark the edge of a day with a tasbih? Day four hundred eighty, and a new surah.

Turn on a tap and fill a glass. It takes three seconds, and where water is cheap it costs almost nothing, so it's easy to forget what's in your hand. Leave a plant without it and it droops. Go without it yourself and you won't last long. Surah twenty-one, Al-Anbiya, the Prophets, in the middle of a long argument about God, stops on a short line about the stuff in that glass.

Al-Anbiya is named for the prophets; it walks through many of them in turn, Ibrahim, Musa, Dawud, Sulayman, Ayyub, Yunus and more. But before the prophets, it points at the world. Verse thirty, in Pickthall's words, asks: "Have not those who disbelieve known that the heavens and the earth were of one piece, then We parted them, and we made every living thing of water?" And it ends: will they not then believe? Look at the shape. A question, then a sign, then another question. The verse isn't giving a lecture. It's asking people to look at what's already in front of them. Some modern readers connect the verse with what biology says about water and life; other scholars caution against reading the Qur'an as a science textbook, since its own purpose here is a sign that leads to faith. Both are said within the tradition. What the verse plainly says is this: life comes from water, and water comes from God. Another verse, in An-Nur, says God created every animal from water: some go on their bellies, some on two legs, some on four. And in Muslim practice, water comes before prayer: wudu: washing the hands, mouth, nose, face and arms, wiping the head, washing the feet. A hadith in Abu Dawud says Muslims are partners in three things: water, pasture and fire. Water isn't meant to be hoarded. So this one line holds three things at once: a sign of the Creator, a gift to all living things, and a trust to be shared. The glass from the tap is all three.
screen: `QUESTION, SIGN, QUESTION.` · `LIFE FROM WATER, WATER FROM GOD.` · `WUDU: WATER BEFORE PRAYER.` · `PARTNERS IN WATER.` · then, large: `EVERY LIVING THING OF WATER.`

segments.voice: Pour a glass of water, or picture one. Hold it. Notice the weight, the temperature, the light through it. Think back along its road: rain, a river or a reservoir, pipes, the tap. Muslim custom, drawn from hadith, is to say bismillah before drinking and to drink in three sips, sitting down. If you'd like, try that: three slow sips. Feel each one go down. Then sit with the empty glass, and let the thanks be wordless. The bell holds the time.
Every living thing from water. A sign in Al-Anbiya, verse thirty: life comes from water, and both come from God. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: from water, life. Today, drink one glass of water slowly, and don't waste any water you could save. Day four hundred eighty.

howItsDone: Muslims make wudu with water before prayer, and some follow the Prophet's practice of saying bismillah and drinking in three sips while seated; 21:30 is often cited when teaching care for water.

options: the Creator who made every living thing from water.

what it means: the verse sets water as a sign that should lead people to faith, between two questions.
what a scholar hears: 21:30 pairs ratq and fatq, the joined and the parted, for heavens and earth; scholars differ on how far to read modern science into it.
